title: Sita
hook: a captive in a grove puts a blade of grass between herself and a king, and later turns down her own rescue

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita: told to stay behind, she argued, promised to tread down the thorns, and walked into exile beside Rama. Did you say a few words of your own today? Day one thousand three hundred thirty.

A single blade of grass. In Valmiki's fifth book, the Sundara Kanda, that's what Sita sets down between herself and Ravana. She's a captive in his city of Lanka, kept in a grove of ashoka trees, guarded day and night. He comes to her with jewels, promises, and threats. She doesn't look at him. She picks up a blade of grass, places it between them, and speaks to the grass. Today: two choices Sita makes in the grove, both in her own words, and the second is a no to the one who has come to find her.
screen: `A SINGLE BLADE OF GRASS.` → `A CAPTIVE IN THE ASHOKA GROVE.` → `TWO CHOICES, IN HER OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: The first choice is the grass. Ravana offers her his kingdom and his queens as her servants. Sita answers through the blade of grass, in paraphrase: turn your mind back to your own wives. I am not for you, the way the light is not for anyone but the sun. Give me back to Rama, if you want to live. The grass is a wall made of almost nothing. It says: I won't even speak to you face to face. The second choice comes later, and it's stranger. Hanuman, Rama's messenger, slips into the grove. He shows her Rama's ring so she knows he's real. And then he makes the obvious offer. Climb on my back, he says. I'll carry you across the sea tonight. Sita says no. She gives reasons, and the text keeps them. You might drop me over the water, she says, or be attacked while carrying me. I won't willingly touch the body of any man but Rama. And this is Rama's to finish: let him come, defeat Ravana, and take me back himself, as a hero should. Then she gives Hanuman a jewel from her hair and a private memory from the forest, so Rama will know the message is truly from her. Here's what's worth carrying from the grove. Sita is the captive, and she is still the one choosing. She sets the terms of her own conversation with Ravana, and the terms of her own rescue. Valmiki could have written a woman simply waiting. He wrote one who keeps deciding.
screen: `SHE SPEAKS THROUGH A BLADE OF GRASS` · `THE RING, AND THE OFFER OF A RIDE` · `SITA SAYS NO, AND GIVES REASONS` · `THE CAPTIVE KEEPS DECIDING`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set down one blade of grass. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that keeps pressing on you, a voice, a habit, a worry. You don't have to fight it. Just picture a single blade of grass set down between you and it. A small, quiet boundary. Breathe on your side of it. Notice that you can still choose where your attention goes. If you pray, you can hold that space before God. The bell holds the time.
Sita. In the ashoka grove, she speaks to Ravana through a blade of grass and turns down Hanuman's offer to carry her home. Today's word.
Your line: Sita. Today, when something presses on you, set down a small boundary, a blade of grass, and choose from your side of it. Day one thousand three hundred thirty.

howItsDone: The Sundara Kanda, the book of Hanuman's journey and Sita in the grove, is recited on its own by some Hindus as a devotional reading, and Sita in the ashoka grove is a familiar scene in temple art and Ram Lila.

he offers to, and she says no. she wants Rama to come and win her back himself.
Sita speaks to Ravana through a blade of grass
she sets it between them and won't speak to him face to face.
Sita sends Rama a private memory so he'll trust the message

fork.setup: you're Sita, a captive in Lanka. Rama's messenger has found you and offers to carry you across the sea tonight. what do you do?
options: climb on and go at once.
say no, and send a token back to Rama.
fork.reveal: she refuses, gives her reasons, and sends a jewel and a private memory. this is Rama's to finish, she says.

original.note: Sanskrit: the ashoka tree. Sita is held in a grove of them in Lanka.

trapdoor: what you thought: in Lanka, Sita simply waits to be rescued.
what it means: in Valmiki, she speaks to Ravana through a blade of grass and turns down Hanuman's offer to carry her home.
what a scholar hears: her reasons are spelled out in the Sundara Kanda: the risk at sea, touching no man but Rama, and Rama's own duty.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 20–21 (Ravana's offer; Sita places a blade of grass between them and answers)
Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 36 (Hanuman gives Rama's ring)
Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 37 (Hanuman's offer to carry her; Sita's refusal and reasons)
Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 38 (the crow story as a private token; the jewel from her hair)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the vulgate; please confirm (critical edition numbering differs).
Sundara 21: confirm the blade-of-grass detail and the paraphrase of Sita's reply (turn to your own wives; she belongs to Rama as light to the sun; return her if you wish to live).

Sundara 37: confirm Sita's reasons for refusing Hanuman (fear of falling into the sea; attack by rakshasas; she will not willingly touch another man's body; it befits Rama to defeat Ravana and take her back).
Sundara 38: the 'private memory' is the crow episode; it is not retold here to keep length. Confirm the jewel (chudamani) detail.
Original: the etymology of ashoka (without sorrow) was deliberately left out under the claims rule.
howItsDone: Sundara Kanda recited as a devotional reading by some Hindus; confirm.
Editor pass: the hook said Sita's refusal 'surprises even Hanuman', which the text does not say; reworded so the hook claims only the refusal.
